item.title: Fuzzy vectors from first and second moments: Affine consistency, carrying and sparsest realizations
item.description: arXiv:2611.31351v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When the probability law of a random vector cannot be identified, its mean and possibly singular covariance can often still be elicited. We consider fuzzy vectors with compact convex cuts as mathematically tractable representations of such a moment pair, and ask how they must be designed to rely only on this information. We postulate two modeling desiderata, independence of the choice of origin and basis, and invariance under embeddings into a higher-dimensional space. Under these requirements alone we show that, in every ambient dimension, every level set of the fuzzy vector must be a Mahalanobis ellipsoid centered at the mean. Its complete specification then amounts to the choice of a radial profile for each covariance rank. We call a fuzzy vector a carrier of the moment pair if at least one of its random-set selections has exactly the given mean and covariance. For an ellipsoidal fuzzy vector of rank $p\ge1$ with radial profile $\rho$, carrying is equivalent to $\int_0^1\rho(\alpha)^2d\alpha\ge p$, and equality characterizes the inclusion-minimal carriers within the fixed-shape Mahalanobis class. A discrete random vector with the same mean and covariance and the fewest equally weighted atoms has its atoms on a regular simplex in Mahalanobis coordinates. Completing this simplex under the rotations left free by the moments yields the minimum-volume crisp ellipsoid in the state space that carries them. The ellipsoidal representation also encodes interaction through the covariance matrix.
item.dc:creator: Jan Schneider, Paul Schneider

item.title: Sharp Hellinger Risk of the Multivariate Gaussian NPMLE
item.description: arXiv:2611.31728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For multivariate Gaussian location mixtures whose mixing distributions have coordinatewise sub-Gaussian tails, we prove that the unconstrained nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator attains the minimax rate $(\log n)^d/n$ under squared Hellinger loss. This holds for every fixed dimension $d\geq2$ and every fixed tail parameter $\sigma>0$. The upper bound applies to every measurable choice of a global likelihood maximizer and improves the earlier bound of order $(\log n)^{d+1}/n$ by a factor of $\log n$. A key step is a sharp bracketing bound for multivariate polynomials. For the $L^2(\rho)$ unit ball of real polynomials in $d$ variables with total degree at most $m$, the log bracketing number at width $\varepsilon$ is at most $\binom{m+d}{d}\log(C_d/\varepsilon)$ for $0<\varepsilon\leq1$. The constant $C_d$ depends only on $d$. The bound holds for every positive Borel measure $\rho$ under which each nonzero polynomial in the space has a finite, positive $L^2(\rho)$ norm. We prove the bound using volume estimates for a complex Veronese cone and Gaussian small-ball probabilities, then apply it to bound the local Hellinger bracketing entropy of Gaussian mixture densities. We obtain the matching minimax lower bound by adapting the Hermite perturbation construction of Kim and Guntuboyina.
item.dc:creator: Xingzhou Wang, Zheng Li

item.title: Asymptotic Normality of the Pearson Correlation between Two Weakly Dependent Random Fields
item.description: arXiv:2611.31743v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the asymptotic behavior of the sample Pearson correlation coefficient between two weakly dependent random fields on a lattice of any fixed dimension. Under strict stationarity, $(BL,\theta)$-weak dependence and mild moment conditions, we establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the estimator on regularly growing domains, which need not be rectangular, with an asymptotic variance expressed through joint fourth-order moments. When the correlation is zero, asymptotic normality holds under weaker conditions. When the fields are independent, the asymptotic variance simplifies to a sum over spatial lags of products of their autocorrelations. The variance approximations behind the classic modified $t$-test, although derived for independent Gaussian fields, target the right variance even without Gaussianity. We also give sufficient conditions for asymptotic normality that are easy to check and cover bounded, Gaussian, $m$-dependent and independent fields. For Gaussian fields, summable auto- and cross-covariances suffice. These conditions rely on new closure results. Squares and products, although not Lipschitz, preserve $(BL,\theta)$-dependence for Gaussian fields, and products of independent fields do so when one is positively or negatively associated. Finally, we propose kernel-based estimators of the asymptotic variance, enabling inference without Gaussianity or parametric spatial models. Simulation studies illustrate their finite-sample performance.
item.dc:creator: Jiyue Qin, Armin Schwartzman, Samuel Davenport

item.title: A General Framework for Identifying the Joint Potential Outcome Distribution through Support Restrictions
item.description: arXiv:2611.31900v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many causal estimands depend on the joint distribution of potential outcomes, which is generally not identifiable because only one potential outcome can be observed for each unit. To obtain identification, researchers often impose assumptions such as monotonicity and exclusion restriction that constrain the support of this joint distribution. For treatments and outcomes that each take finitely many values, we define a similarity matrix whose entries count, for each pair of potential outcome strata, the number of treatments yielding the same outcome. We then prove that, under unconfoundedness, identification holds if and only if this matrix is invertible, yielding a criterion directly verifiable from the support. In addition, we derive an identification formula for the joint distribution under these support restrictions and show that an average causal estimand is identifiable if and only if its integrand admits an additive representation on the restricted support. Finally, we derive sharp testable implications of the support restriction. Our results unify and generalize a broad range of identification results in the literature.
item.dc:creator: Benedikt Koch, Kosuke Imai

item.title: Certified minimax normal-scale mixtures for the logistic-normal integral
item.description: arXiv:2611.32270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The logistic distribution function is a scale mixture of normal distribution functions, and Monahan and Stefanski approximate it by the $K$-term mixture $\Lambda(x) \approx \sum_{i} w_i \Phi(s_i x)$ chosen to minimise the uniform error on the real line. Each such mixture reduces the logistic-normal integral to a sum of $K$ normal distribution functions with the mixture's uniform error bound. This integral is the expectation of a logistic sigmoid over a normal distribution in statistics and the Gauss-Fermi integral in semiconductor physics. Monahan and Stefanski tabulate constants for $K \le 8$ and conjecture that the optimal error equioscillates at $2K$ points, while above $K = 8$ the Remez exchange and local solvers stall at nonequioscillating stationary points. We prove that the tangent space of the mixture family is a Chebyshev system, which forces $2K$-point equioscillation at every interior minimiser and makes any such solution the unique global minimax, and we prove interior attainment for $K \le 11$. A certification algorithm audits a candidate mixture in multiple-precision arithmetic, using a proved bound on the number of extrema as its completeness test, and three search pipelines reach $K = 9, 10, 11$, the last with certified worst-case error $1.26 \times 10^{-11}$. A signed $K = 22$ mixture carries a relaxed certificate at $3.605 \times 10^{-15}$. In causal mediation with a binary outcome, the certified sum replaces a biased Taylor expansion and stochastic integration with one closed-form evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Ruijie Li

item.title: Admissibility of Linear Time Series Models under Cone Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2611.32414v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time series analysis extends beyond vector-valued observations to evolving probability densities, quantile functions, and covariance operators. These objects carry intrinsic constraints, raising questions about the admissibility of additive linear models, which have long served as a foundation for time series modelling and theory. We give a necessary and sufficient support condition for a stationary Hilbert-space linear process to remain in a closed convex cone almost surely. Innovations with unbounded lower tails, including Gaussian innovations, confine randomness to the cone's largest linear subspace. For fractional filters with convergent normalized cumulative coefficients, the leading stochastic directions obey the same restriction, even with bounded innovations. For real-line quantiles, variation under unbounded lower tails and leading fractional accumulation can occur only through location shifts. For cone-valued processes, partial sums of centred stationary increments remain bounded in mean square when evaluated by any linear functional that is nonnegative on the cone, in contrast to the growing variance of a random walk. We derive an exact slope criterion for locally absolutely continuous quantiles and construct nondegenerate additive models with bounded innovations for quantiles, densities, and covariance matrices. These findings clarify the scope of ordinary additive modelling under structural constraints.
item.dc:creator: Won-Ki Seo

item.title: Recursive estimation of the Oja median and related simplex medians
item.description: arXiv:2611.32604v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the recursive estimation of multivariate location functionals defined by minimizing the expected volume of a random simplex. This framework encompasses both the spatial median and the affine-equivariant Oja median. We introduce a sliding-window stochastic gradient algorithm and its averaged version, and establish their strong consistency and asymptotic normality. We further show that the sliding-window approach offers a favorable trade-off between statistical accuracy and computational cost compared with a naive disjoint-block stochastic gradient algorithm and offline methods, with the statistical comparison based on asymptotic covariances. Numerical experiments illustrate the computational advantages of the proposed procedures and their finite-sample accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Antoine Godichon-Baggioni (LPSM), Guillaume Sall{\'e} (LMI, LPSM)

item.title: A Dimension-Free Bound on the FDR of the Benjamini-Hochberg Procedure under Slowly Decaying Gaussian Correlations
item.description: arXiv:2611.32898v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure is proven to control the false discovery rate under independence and under positive dependence. Under arbitrary dependence, however, its guarantee deteriorates by a factor that grows logarithmically with the number of hypotheses. For Gaussian test statistics, it is unknown whether dependence can make the false discovery rate grow with the number of tests. We study this question when the correlation between two test statistics decays with the distance between their indices. We seek guarantees that hold uniformly over a wide class of correlation structures and over all configurations of the signals. We show that if the correlations decay at least as fast as a power of the inverse logarithm of the distance with exponent larger than one, then the false discovery rate of the original BH procedure is bounded by the nominal level times a factor that does not depend on the number of hypotheses. This factor grows only polylogarithmically as the level decreases. The result holds for both one- and two-sided tests, and the procedure uses no knowledge of the correlations. The class allows correlations of both signs. The required decay can be arbitrarily close to the inverse logarithm. The key technical tool is a truncated Hermite expansion of the exceedance indicators. It shows that their main fluctuations are common to all thresholds that BH may use. These fluctuations can be well controlled, while the remainder is too small to accumulate, which leads to a bound that does not inflate with the dimension.
item.dc:creator: Zuofeng Shang, Wenge Guo

item.title: Efficient inferential models and their fiducial connections
item.description: arXiv:2611.32930v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Valid inferential models (IMs) provide frequentist calibration guarantees, but validity alone does not determine which construction is most informative. We study finite-sample efficiency through concentration risk, the expected volume under a possibility contour. For a smooth, fully identified association and a specified parameter-volume measure, a weighted Neyman--Pearson argument identifies the generalized fiducial density as the optimal score for minimizing cut volume subject to fixed-data auxiliary compatibility. The resulting maximum-specificity transform gives an explicit volume interpretation of the fiducial efficiency ceiling, which need not itself be sampling valid. We develop two approaches to valid construction. The first minimizes design-averaged concentration risk among single, data-independent auxiliary-compatible contours. The design measure prioritizes efficiency without requiring prior beliefs or restricting validity. The second localizes the parameter-volume score to candidate-specific contours, yielding a normalized, valid IM equivalent to sampling validification of the relative fiducial likelihood. A parallel sample-space construction recovers the ordinary likelihood-ratio IM; direct validification of the ceiling provides another repair. For the same association, exact, data-independent predictive contours share a common fiducial distribution as a saturating inner probability, while generating different calibrated confidence-region geometries. Design averaging thus selects an efficient member without changing the underlying fiducial law. Examples in a two-component measurement model and an exponential scale model illustrate the efficiency gains and show that sampling-valid repair can improve on the raw ceiling by leaving the fixed-data auxiliary-compatible class over which it is optimal.
item.dc:creator: Max Raner

item.title: Agent Evaluation Without Ground Truth: A Null Proportion Perspective
item.description: arXiv:2611.31539v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The correctness of actions taken by agents is typically evaluated against known, externally verified ground truth labels, such as whether a proof is correct or whether code compiles and passes unit tests. However, as coding and science agents are entrusted with more end-to-end autonomy -- proposing interventions, running experiments, and deciding what to deploy and investigate next -- whether an agent's actions genuinely improve an outcome must be inferred from noisy, often inconclusive experiments. To evaluate agents in this setting, we define agent quality as a weighted sum of correct decisions along its trajectory, using sequences of $e$-values as statistical evidence regarding correctness in place of ground-truth labels. Our framework accommodates arbitrarily dependent decisions, data-dependent trajectory termination, dynamically generated hypotheses, and quality measures defined after the trajectory concludes. We construct upper and lower bound estimators and confidence sets for agent quality with statistical guarantees that hold uniformly over agent trajectory distributions and establish instance-wise sharpness of our estimator class. We demonstrate our methods with a case study comparing the success of Claude Opus and Claude Haiku in improving the runtime of an open-source Python package.
item.dc:creator: Brian M. Cho, Michael Lindon, Nathan Kallus

item.title: Aalen-Johansen as an augmented IPCW estimator
item.description: arXiv:2611.32026v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We show that, in every sample, the widely used Aalen-Johansen estimator of a state occupation probability is an inverse probability of censoring weighted estimator augmented by a working Markov prediction from each subject's current state. This identity explains the robustness of the Aalen-Johansen against departures from the Markov assumption. It also reveals that its influence function differs from the semiparametric efficient one by two orthogonal components: the information in earlier history beyond the current state, and the error of the Markov prediction. Based on this decomposition, we propose a practical, model-free least-squares augmentation of the Aalen-Johansen that regresses the outcome on a history score, narrowing the gap under non-Markov processes without increasing the asymptotic variance. Its advantages are validated both theoretically and in simulations.
item.dc:creator: Lu Mao

item.title: From the ELBO to Maximum Likelihood: Convergence of Variational Autoencoders for Nonlinear Mixed-Effects Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2611.32372v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Nonlinear mixed-effects (NLME) models are the central statistical models of pharmacometrics, where they support dose selection, individualized dosing and regulatory decisions in drug development. Statistically, NLME modeling is a marginalized likelihood problem. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) solve such problems with a neural network encoder that amortizes the approximation of the intractable posterior distribution, and allow the integration of AI components into NLME modeling. This paper provides the convergence analysis of the VAE-NLME algorithm. First, its version for the evidence lower bound (ELBO) is proven to converge almost surely to the set of stationary points of the ELBO, without assuming that the encoder is trained exactly. Second, the final VAE-NLME algorithm trains the encoder on the ELBO by gradient-based optimization and uses it as proposal for importance-weighted sufficient statistics. It converges almost surely to the set of stationary points of the marginal log-likelihood, without any assumption on the training of the encoder. Thus, it combines the fast gradient-based training of VAEs with the limit of maximum likelihood estimation.
item.dc:creator: Jan Rohleff, Johannes Schropp

item.title: Quadratic Wasserstein transport for elliptical distributions
item.description: arXiv:2611.32773v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The quadratic Wasserstein distance between Gaussian distributions is given by the classical Bures-Wasserstein formula, which depends only on the means, the covariance matrices $\Sigma_0$ and $\Sigma_1$, and their interaction $K=(\Sigma_0^{1/2}\Sigma_1\Sigma_0^{1/2})^{1/2}$. The same formula holds for elliptical distributions with a common radial law. In this paper, we extend this representation to general elliptical distributions by identifying an additional transport cost $\Gamma$ that depends on the radial laws and the spectrum of $K$. We describe $\Gamma$ via a weighted quadratic transport problem involving Dirichlet distributions and show that optimal couplings preserve directions within the eigenspaces of $K$. When $K$ has a single eigenvalue, we obtain an explicit cost formula and an optimal Monge map. For general spectra, we derive remarkably tight lower and upper bounds for $\Gamma$ using nested spectral projections and Knothe-Rosenblatt couplings. The lower bound is based on one-dimensional integrals and can be computed fast. For Gaussian, Student-$t$, uniform ball, and uniform sphere distributions, the upper bound also admits computationally efficient representations via dynamic programming. Numerical experiments demonstrate that we reduce the gap between the previously known bounds by more than 80% in many settings, and by over 99.9% in certain scenarios, even in dimension $10^6$. These improvements are particularly valuable in high-dimensional or heavy-tailed settings, where accurate numerical computation of quadratic Wasserstein distances is challenging.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Ansari, Ludger R\"uschendorf

item.title: Online V-Learning with Adaptive Longitudinal Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.32947v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning methods for estimating optimal dynamic treatment regimes are increasingly applied in mobile health (mHealth), where treatment decisions are made continually. Luckett et al. (2020) proposed V-learning, which estimates an optimal policy from offline trajectories. In practice, mHealth policies are updated online. Batch updating, in which the policy is re-estimated after each block of new data, is a tractable middle ground between offline learning and updating after every observation. However, because each batch's treatment policy is estimated from data pooled across patients in earlier batches, the resulting data are adaptively collected and patient trajectories are dependent, a setting that offline theory does not address. We develop statistical theory for V-learning in this setting with varying, deterministic batch sizes. For each fixed batch, as the number of patients grows, we establish uniform consistency of the estimated value function, consistency of the estimated policy, a functional central limit theorem over the policy class, asymptotic normality of the estimated value of the learned policy, and a consistent variance estimator. To first order, the online procedure performs as well as an oracle that deploys the optimal policy after the first batch. With the number of patients fixed and the number of batches growing, the estimated value function and policy remain consistent under a persistent identifiability condition. In simulations, as the number of patients grows with the number of batches fixed, confidence intervals attain near-nominal coverage under adaptive assignment and the online procedure closely matches the oracle. With a small cohort followed over many batches, the learned policies improve steadily.
item.dc:creator: Aniruddhan Ganesaraman, Michael R. Kosorok

item.title: On importance sampling and independent Metropolis-Hastings with an unbounded weight function
item.description: arXiv:2411.09514v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Importance sampling and independent Metropolis-Hastings are among the fundamental building blocks of Monte Carlo methods. Both require a proposal distribution that globally approximates the target distribution, and pointwise evaluation of the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the target distribution relative to the proposal, also called the weight function. We study the bias of importance sampling and independent Metropolis-Hastings, without assuming that the weight function is bounded. We show that the common random numbers coupling of independent Metropolis-Hastings is maximal. Using that coupling, we derive polynomial bounds on the total variation distance of the chain to its target distribution. We further consider bias removal techniques using couplings, and provide conditions under which the resulting unbiased estimators have finite moments, and under which their efficiency is comparable to that of importance sampling. Experiments illustrate unbiased estimators of the inverse of a normalizing constant, estimators of nested expectations, and combination of importance sampling with robust mean estimation methods.
item.dc:creator: George Deligiannidis (University of Oxford), Pierre E. Jacob (ESSEC Business School), El Mahdi Khribch (ESSEC Business School), Guanyang Wang (Rutgers University)

item.title: The Threshold Breakdown Point
item.description: arXiv:2605.04317v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a novel approach to finite sample robustness that avoids the pessimism of traditional breakdown analyses. We define the threshold breakdown point, the smallest contamination fraction needed to induce a prescribed deviation, and the finite sample $m$-sensitivity, the worst-case deviation that an estimator can incur after $m$ observations are contaminated. We derive these measures for commonly used $M$-estimators, their standard errors and related test statistics. This allows us to extend the decision breakdown point of Zhang (1996) to obtain general breakdown characterizations for hypothesis testing, and show how these notions connect to finite sample counterparts of the power and level breakdown functions of He, Simpson and Portnoy (1990). We complement our work with an inferential framework for the threshold breakdown and $m$-sensitivity that yields consistency and asymptotic normality results, as well as a valid multiplier bootstrap for uncertainty quantification. We illustrate the practical utility of our methods in various numerical examples and an application to a two sample testing problem for a blood pressure dataset.
item.dc:creator: Tianjun Ke, Marco Avella Medina

item.title: An adaptive $L_2$-type test for high-dimensional white noise
item.description: arXiv:2609.33418v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a new $L_2$-type test for white noise which allows the dimension $p$ of the time series to either (i) be a fixed constant, or (ii) diverge with the sample size $n$. The proposed test statistic exhibits an interesting phase transition, following two different regimes of behavior: $p$ is fixed, and $p\rightarrow\infty$. Because identification of the operable regime is difficult, if not impossible in practice, we devise a novel adaptive bootstrap method to construct a unified testing procedure across different phases. Numerical experiments confirm the good finite sample performance of the proposed adaptive $L_2$-type test in comparison to the existing methods in the literature. The proposed testing procedure has been implemented in R package HDTSA.
item.dc:creator: Jinyuan Chang, Jing He, Weiming Li, Chen Lin

item.title: On the median of the beta distribution in relation to the median of the gamma distribution
item.description: arXiv:2610.39202v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The median of the beta distribution has no closed form, but it is closely tied to the median of the gamma distribution. Kerman's approximation has the ratio form $g(\alpha)/(g(\alpha)+g(\beta))$ with $g(x) = x - 1/3$, a lower bound on the gamma median, and it is a lower bound on the beta median for $1/3 < \alpha < \beta$. The ratio form built from the true gamma median is a tighter lower bound, asymptotically exact as $\beta \to \infty$. The ratio form built from the Wilson-Hilferty approximation to the gamma median, implicit in a classical approximation to the $F$ distribution but little known as an approximation to the beta median, is an upper bound on the line $\alpha = 1$ and, along each ray $\beta = r\alpha$ with $r > 1$, for large shape parameters. The ratio form that is exact on the lines $\alpha = 1$ and $\beta = 1$, $(2^{1/\beta} - 1)/(2^{1/\alpha} + 2^{1/\beta} - 2)$, is numerically within 0.3% of the median when both shape parameters are at least 1, and provably less than 25% above it for $\alpha \le \beta$; it yields a new approximation to the gamma median, which is an upper bound on it for shape parameter below 1 and a lower bound above 1. Interpolating between it and a ratio form with a $1/x$ correction gives, with no fitted constant, an approximation within 0.016% of the median when both shape parameters are at least 1. No ratio form gives the beta median exactly. For large shape parameters, the logit of the median has an explicit second-order expansion. For small shape parameters, bounds in elementary functions are asymptotically tight. An approximation in elementary functions that joins the two ends, with four fitted constants, is exact on the lines $\alpha = 1$, $\beta = 1$, and $\alpha = \beta$, and numerically within 0.065% of the median over the whole domain. Most of the proofs are machine-verified in Lean 4.
item.dc:creator: Richard F. Lyon

item.title: Perfect Clustering in Extremely Sparse Multilayer Networks with Groupwise Subspace Structure
item.description: arXiv:2507.19423v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The paper studies a multilayer network on the same collection of nodes, where each layer follows the Generalized Random Dot Product Graph Model. Furthermore, all layers can be partitioned into groups, each group with its own unique latent subspace structure, but otherwise the matrices of connection probabilities can all be different. This setting is extremely general and includes most multilayer network models as special cases. In addition, we are interested in the situation where the layer networks may be extremely sparse and, therefore, the layer-by-layer analysis is unreliable. This problem can also be seen as a generalization of the classic setting in which one recovers a shared structure across an entire collection of matrices, extending it to the case where such structures are shared only within specific groups of matrices. The key task in this setting is to recover the groups of layers with unique subspace structures, since, after that, the information in those groups of layers can be pooled together by well-studied methods. Until now, clustering of layers in such networks was based on layer-by-layer analysis, which required the multilayer network to be sufficiently dense. Our paper is the first to provide a tensor-based approach to the problem that combines information from all layers in an unconventional manner. Our theoretical results, established under intuitive and non-restrictive assumptions, assert that the new technique achieves perfect clustering under sparsity conditions that, up to logarithmic factors, coincide with the computational lower bound derived for a much simpler model. The paper also delivers a nuanced message about the applicability of the new technique.
item.dc:creator: Marianna Pensky

item.title: Optimal Algorithms for Nonlinear Estimation with Convex Models
item.description: arXiv:2512.20826v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A linear functional of an object from a convex symmetric set can be optimally estimated, in a worst-case sense, by a linear functional of observations made on the object. This well-known fact is extended here to a nonlinear setting: other simple functionals of the object can be optimally estimated by functionals of the observations that share a similar simple structure. This is established for the maximum of several linear functionals and even for the $\ell$th largest among them. Proving the latter requires an unusual variation of the analytical Hahn--Banach theorem. The existence results are accompanied by practical recipes relying on convex optimization to construct the desired functionals, thereby justifying the term of estimation algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Simon Foucart

item.title: Uniform Maximum Projection Designs for Computer Experiments
item.description: arXiv:2603.19778v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Space-filling experimental designs are widely used in engineering computer experiments, where only a limited number of expensive model evaluations can be afforded. Distance-based designs such as Maximin or Minimax ensure global space-filling, while Latin hypercube sampling enforces uniform one-dimensional projections, yet neither guarantees uniformity in lowdimensional subspaces. Maximum Projection (MaxPro) designs were introduced to improve uniformity in low-dimensional subspaces, yet their original formulation relies on the Euclidean distance and may induce systematic density distortions in bounded domains. We demonstrate that the standard MaxPro criterion leads to statistically non-uniform sampling, resulting in undersampling of corner regions and biased Monte Carlo estimates. To remedy this issue, we introduce a periodic variant of the criterion, termed Uniform Maximum Projection (uMaxPro), in which the Euclidean metric is replaced by a periodic distance based on the minimum image convention. The proposed uMaxPro designs preserve the projection-aware structure of MaxPro while achieving statistical uniformity of the design-generation mechanism. Numerical experiments show unbiased Monte Carlo integration with reduced variance, excellent subspace projection performance, and competitive discrepancy properties. The methodology is further validated on benchmark engineering problems, including a meso-scale finite element model of concrete, demonstrating improved accuracy in surrogate modeling and probabilistic estimation. The resulting criterion provides a simple and computationally efficient modification of MaxPro that enhances its robustness for nonadaptive computer experiments. The construction algorithm, open-source implementation, and reproducible optimized designs are provided to facilitate practical adoption of the method.
item.dc:creator: Miroslav Vo\v{r}echovsk\'y, Jan Ma\v{s}ek

item.title: List Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2603.25280v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Classical estimation outputs a single point estimate of an unknown $d$-dimensional vector from an observation. In this paper, we study \emph{$k$-list estimation}, in which a single observation is used to produce a list of $k$ candidate estimates and performance is measured by the expected squared distance from the true vector to the closest candidate. We compare this centralized setting with a symmetric decentralized MMSE benchmark in which $k$ agents observe conditionally i.i.d.\ measurements and each agent outputs its own MMSE estimate. On the centralized side, we show that optimal $k$-list estimation is equivalent to fixed-rate $k$-point vector quantization of the posterior distribution and, under standard regularity conditions, admits an exact high-rate asymptotic expansion with explicit constants and decay rate $k^{-2/d}$. On the decentralized side, we derive lower bounds in terms of the small-ball behavior of the single-agent MMSE error; in particular, when the conditional error density is bounded near the origin, the benchmark distortion cannot decay faster than order $k^{-2/d}$. We further show that if the error density vanishes at the origin in a power-law fashion, then the decentralized benchmark is provably unable to match the centralized $k^{-2/d}$ exponent, whereas the centralized estimator retains the $k^{-2/d}$ scaling. Gaussian specializations yield explicit formulas and numerical experiments corroborate the predicted asymptotic behavior. Overall, the results show that, in the scaling with $k$, one observation combined with $k$ carefully chosen candidates can be asymptotically as effective as---and in some regimes strictly better than---this MMSE-based decentralized benchmark with $k$ \rev{conditionally independent} observations.
item.dc:creator: Nikola Zlatanov, Amin Gohari, Farzad Shahrivari, Mikhail Rudakov

item.title: Robust stochastic first order methods in heavy-tailed noise via medoid mini-batch gradient sampling
item.description: arXiv:2605.07634v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We consider a first order stochastic optimization framework where, at each iteration, $K$ independent identically distributed (i.i.d.) data point samples are drawn, based on which stochastic gradients can be queried. We allow gradient noise to be heavy-tailed, with possibly infinite variances. For the considered heavy-tailed setting, many algorithmic variants have recently been proposed based on gradient clipping or other nonlinear operators (e.g., normalization) applied over noisy gradients. In this paper, we take an alternative approach and propose a novel gradient estimator. The core idea of proposed estimator is to split the $K$-sized data batch into $M$ distinct data chunks, form for each chunk the stochastic gradient, and select the stochastic gradient of the chunk that is medoid of gradients of all data-chunks. For a broad class of symmetric heavy-tailed gradient noise distributions, we show that the proposed estimator has a finite second moment even when the underlying gradient noise has an infinite second moment. For nonconvex objectives, this yields convergence to a neighborhood of zero in expected squared gradient norm at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1})$. We explicitly characterize the size of this neighborhood in terms of the noise and algorithm parameters. When the time horizon $T$ is known in advance, we establish an $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2})$ convergence rate. A diminishing step size achieves the same rate up to a logarithmic factor. Incorporating clipping or a more general nonlinear transformation yields high-probability convergence guarantees with the same rate up to logarithmic factors. Experimental results indicate that R-SGD-Mini and its clipped or nonlinear variant consistently perform favorably compared to SGD, clipped SGD, Nonlinear SGD and Median-of-Means based methods.
item.dc:creator: Manojlo Vukovic, Dusan Jakovetic

item.title: Exponential Smoothing for Time Series of Random Objects
item.description: arXiv:2609.20274v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Time series of random objects, such as covariance matrices, probability distributions, and functional data, call for forecasting methods that do not rely on arithmetic operations. We introduce geodesic exponential smoothing for time series in Hadamard spaces. The forecast level moves a fixed fraction of the way along the geodesic towards each new observation. The smoothing parameter is estimated by minimising the average squared distance between observations and forecasts. The method involves a single scalar parameter, assumes no stationarity, and updates online in constant time per observation. We further introduce an innovations mechanism under which each observation has conditional Fr\'echet mean equal to the current level, the metric-space analogue of the innovations state-space model. We show via the quasilinearisation of Hadamard spaces that the level is a martingale in a nonlinear sense, that the spread of the data from the initial state grows at least linearly in time, and that their quasi-autocorrelation at any fixed lag tends to one. We prove almost-sure consistency and asymptotic normality of the smoothing-parameter estimator. Three real-data applications, spanning covariance-matrix, distributional, and functional time series, assess the forecasting performance against structurally heavier alternatives.

item.title: Anytime-valid goodness-of-fit test by $e$-spacings
item.description: arXiv:2611.23775v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: To perform an anytime-valid goodness-of-fit test, we propose spacing-based $e$-processes that control the type-I error rate under arbitrary stopping rules. Based on the maximum spacing of order statistics, we construct spacing-based $e$-processes for nonparametrically testing distribution. The resulting procedures are simple and computationally efficient, and are power-consistent. We call them $e$-spacing tests. This approach is especially powerful in detecting localized discrepancy between the data-generating density and the null density. Under mild conditions, the logarithm of the proposed $e$-process is asymptotically equivalent to that of the oracle-optimal $e$-process. We further generalize the construction from maximal spacing to maximum spacing set in the form of the $1/k$ fraction of the largest $m$th order spacings, as a measure of the lower-level set of density. It boosts power under more global discrepancy from the null. Furthermore, we propose a greedy predictable scheme, via argmax or softmax rules, to combine multiple $e$-spacing testing strategies. We prove that it optimally tunes the $e$-spacing test. The proposed approach is readily generalizable to multivariate testing via a coordinate-wise Rosenblatt-transform. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed methods perform favorably relative to the considered anytime-valid competitors as well as various types of multiple test-adjusted Kolmogorov--Smirnov tests.
item.dc:creator: Yunda Hao, Kin Wai Chan
